<div class="clt-lesson batch-lesson" data-lesson="correlation"><h2 id="learning-goals">What are we trying to understand?</h2><p><strong>What does a correlation capture, and what does it leave out?</strong></p><p>A hypothetical researcher records study hours and attention scores for ten students. Change the linear pattern, the amount of scatter, the observed range, and an additional unusual observation.</p><div class="clt-overview"><strong>Learning goals</strong><ol><li>Describe direction and strength from a scatterplot.</li><li>Interpret Pearson r as a measure of linear association.</li><li>Investigate outliers and restricted range.</li><li>Distinguish association from causation.</li></ol></div><h2 id="explore">Make a prediction and explore</h2><section class="clt-simulator"><p>Predict whether narrowing the observed range of study hours necessarily leaves r unchanged.</p><div class="controls"><div><label for="slope">Underlying linear pattern: <output id="slope-v">3</output></label><input id="slope" type="range" min="-4" max="4" step="1" value="3"></div><div><label for="noise">Scatter multiplier: <output id="noise-v">2</output></label><input id="noise" type="range" min="1" max="4" step="1" value="2"></div><div><label for="range">Observed study-hour range</label><select id="range"><option value="all">Full range: 1–10 hours</option><option value="restricted">Restricted: 3–8 hours</option></select></div><div><label for="outlier">Additional observation</label><select id="outlier"><option value="none">None</option><option value="high">High score at 11 hours</option><option value="low">Low score at 11 hours</option></select></div></div><div class="metrics"><div class="metric"><span>Pearson r</span><strong id="r">—</strong></div><div class="metric"><span>r²</span><strong id="r2">—</strong></div><div class="metric"><span>Number of observations</span><strong id="n">—</strong></div></div><div id="chart" class="plot"></div><p id="description" role="status"></p><p class="note">Orange dot (if present): additional observation. The axes remain fixed. Data are deterministic examples.</p><details><summary>View paired data</summary><table class="data-table"><caption>Illustrative paired observations</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Student</th><th scope="col">Hours</th><th scope="col">Score</th></tr></thead><tbody id="pairs"></tbody></table></details></section><h2 id="interpret">Interpret what you find</h2><ol><li>Compare slopes +3, 0 and −3 at the same noise level. What changes about the direction?</li><li>Increase noise while holding the slope setting fixed. Compare r and the visual pattern.</li><li>Restrict the range, then restore it. Does r necessarily stay the same?</li><li>Add a high and then a low score at 11 hours. Explain why the position of an unusual point matters.</li></ol><h2 id="explanation">What is the method telling us?</h2><p>Pearson r is the standardized covariance of two quantitative variables. It ranges from −1 to +1. Its sign describes linear direction and its magnitude describes linear strength. A near-zero r does not rule out a nonlinear relationship. Restricted range and unusual observations can change r, sometimes substantially.</p><p>Correlation is symmetric: swapping x and y leaves r unchanged. It does not identify causal direction, rule out confounding, or establish a treatment effect. For example, prior preparation might influence both study hours and attention scores.</p><h2 id="knowledge-check">Check your understanding</h2><p>Choose an answer, then check your reasoning.
